passage:
Monday. Bhavna looked into her daughter's room at seven. Devika had been curled on the bed since lunch, knees up, phone close to her face. When Bhavna asked about dinner, Devika rubbed her neck and snapped, "I said I'm coming!"
Wednesday. Bhavna didn't lecture. She sat on the floor and rolled her own shoulders. "My neck is stiff from the laptop. Stretch with me?" Devika rolled her eyes, then joined in. Together they stacked three old textbooks on the desk so the phone stood at eye level for her online class.
Saturday. A soft timer rang in Devika's room. Bhavna heard her get up, walk to the balcony and swing her arms. At dinner Devika laughed at her brother's joke. "My neck doesn't hurt today," she said, surprised.

qa.q: What did Bhavna and Devika stack on the desk?
qa.a: They stacked three old textbooks so the phone stood at eye level.

qa.q: What was Bhavna thinking when she chose not to lecture on Wednesday?
qa.a: She seemed to worry a lecture would start a fight, so she hoped a shared stretch would reach Devika better than a scolding.

qa.q: What small steps made the difference for Devika?
qa.a: Stretching, raising the phone to eye level and taking breaks when the timer rang eased her neck and her temper.

qa.q: How might Devika have felt on Saturday compared to Monday?
qa.a: On Saturday she felt lighter and surprised that her neck didn't hurt, while on Monday she was sore and irritable.

grounding: It shows a parent noticing a teenager curled over a phone with a stiff neck and a short temper, and how breaks, stretching and a raised screen ease both.

passage:
Shreya, come sit with your Nani Sudha. You think phones invented bad posture? Let me tell you about your Mama when he was fourteen. We bought him one of those handheld game machines, grey, with tiny buttons. He would sit on the steps of our old Nagpur house, bent over it like a question mark, for whole afternoons.
By evening he'd be rubbing his neck and slamming doors. I blamed his age. Your Nana blamed the game.
One day I sat next to him on the steps and asked, "Does your neck hurt, beta?" He admitted it did, every day. So we made a deal: after each level he'd stand up and stretch, and he'd play at the table with the game propped on a book, not on the steps. Within a week, the door slamming nearly stopped.

qa.q: Where did Mama sit to play his game?
qa.a: He would sit on the steps of the old Nagpur house.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel about Mama's bad moods at first, and what did she blame?
qa.a: Sudha was puzzled by his neck-rubbing and door-slamming and blamed his age, never guessing that his sore neck was behind it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Sitting beside him and asking gently whether his neck hurt, which led to a deal about stretching and a better position instead of a fight about the game.

qa.q: How might Mama have felt when Sudha sat beside him and asked about his neck?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved to be asked kindly rather than blamed, which made him willing to admit the pain.

grounding: It shows a parent watching a teenager hunched over a device with a sore neck and bad mood, and how breaks and better position ease body and temper.

passage: The train from Chennai to Delhi was thirty-three hours, and Lavanya, fifteen, spent most of the first day curled on the upper berth over her phone. By evening she was rubbing her neck and snapping at everyone. When Mahima, her mother, asked if she wanted tea, Lavanya said, 'Can you just leave me alone?' There was no room to walk, no signal half the time and the fan barely worked. Mahima noticed how her daughter's head drooped towards the screen. At the next long halt in Nagpur, she tapped the berth. 'Come down. Ten minutes on the platform, then back.' They walked the length of the train and stretched their arms over their heads, laughing at a monkey on the roof. Back inside, Mahima propped Lavanya's phone on a folded shawl at eye level. Lavanya's shoulders loosened, and so did her mood.

qa.q: How long was the train journey from Chennai to Delhi?
qa.a: Thirty-three hours.

qa.q: What was Mahima thinking as she watched Lavanya's head droop?
qa.a: Mahima was concerned, seeing that the hunched posture was making her daughter stiff and grumpy.

qa.q: What did Mahima do that eased Lavanya's neck and mood?
qa.a: She took her for a short walk and stretch at the halt and propped the phone at eye level on a shawl.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt by evening before the walk?
qa.a: She was probably stiff, tired and irritable, wanting to be left alone.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a teenager hunched over a phone for hours with a stiff neck and tired mood, and easing it with a break, stretching and raising the screen.

passage: By Sunday afternoon, Damini, sixteen, had been hunched over her drawing tablet on the bed in their Mumbai flat since breakfast, knees up, chin almost on the screen. When Rehana, her mother, called her for lunch, Damini snapped, 'In a minute!' twice, then came out rubbing her neck and complaining of a headache. Rehana didn't comment on the snapping. After lunch she carried a stack of old encyclopaedias to Damini's desk and set the tablet on top so it was level with her eyes. 'Try drawing here. And every time you finish a layer, walk to the balcony and stretch.' Damini rolled her eyes but tried. By evening she was still drawing, sitting upright. She came out for tea without being called, and even laughed at her brother's joke.

qa.q: What did Rehana stack to raise the tablet?
qa.a: Old encyclopaedias.

qa.q: How did Rehana seem to feel when Damini snapped at lunch?
qa.a: Rehana seemed patient and concerned, choosing not to react to the snapping.

qa.q: Why did raising the tablet help Damini?
qa.a: It let her sit upright, easing the neck strain that was making her tired and irritable.

qa.q: How might Damini's brother have noticed the change?
qa.a: He probably saw a more relaxed sister who laughed at his joke instead of snapping.

grounding: Shows a parent seeing a teenager curled over a device for hours with a stiff neck and short temper, and easing it with a raised screen and stretch breaks.

passage:
'Jasleen, you've been on that phone since two.'
'I'm talking to Noor, Mumma. It's important.'
'Okay. How's your neck?'
Jasleen rubbed it. 'Hurts. And I've got a headache.'
'You're curled up like a prawn.'
'Very funny.'
Aparna sat on the edge of the bed. 'I'm not taking the phone. But will you come and do five minutes of stretches with me? Then you can go back.'
'Mumma…'
'Five minutes. I need a partner for the arm circles.'
Jasleen groaned but followed her to the balcony. They rolled their shoulders, reached for the sky, turned their heads slowly side to side. Jasleen yawned hugely.
'Better?'
'…A bit. Less cranky.'
'Go on, then. Maybe sit at the desk this time?'

qa.q: When did Jasleen start using the phone?
qa.a: Since two.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling as she sat on the edge of the bed?
qa.a: She was concerned about Jasleen's sore neck and headache, and wanted to help without starting a fight.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Aparna invited Jasleen to stretch as a partner instead of taking the phone, so the break felt like company rather than a punishment.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt after the stretches?
qa.a: She felt a bit looser and less cranky, even if she did not want to admit it.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a teen curled over a phone with a stiff neck and cranky mood, and easing it with a stretch break and a better sitting position.

passage: Last winter I kept finding my son Dhruv folded over his phone on the divan, chin almost on his chest, for three or four hours at a stretch. I'm Ramesh, his father, and I'll admit my first move was to shout. That got me a slammed door. Then one evening he rubbed his neck and winced, and snapped at his sister over nothing. I saw that he was tired and sore, not just rude. So I tried something else. I bought a cheap phone stand, put it on the study table at eye level, and asked if he'd stretch with me during the ad breaks of the cricket match. He rolled his eyes, but he did it. Within a couple of weeks the neck-rubbing stopped, and the snapping got rarer. He still loves his phone. He just holds his head up now.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh put the phone stand?
qa.a: On the study table, at eye level.

qa.q: What did Ramesh feel when Dhruv winced, and what did he understand?
qa.a: He felt concerned and a little sorry for shouting, seeing that Dhruv was tired and sore, not just rude.

qa.q: Which of Ramesh's changes worked, and why?
qa.a: The eye-level stand and shared stretches in the ad breaks eased Dhruv's neck without a fight, and his temper improved too.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have seen his father's shouting compared with the stretching invitation?
qa.a: The shouting felt like an attack and got a slammed door, while stretching together felt friendly, so Dhruv went along with it.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a teenager curled over a phone with a stiff neck and short temper, and breaks, stretching and an eye-level screen easing both.
